claim: Reduced structural and functional interhemispheric connectivity correlates with the severity of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) behaviors in humans.
source: Reduced structural and functional interhemispheric connectivity correlates with the severity of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) behaviors in humans.
evidence: This is a general statement about ASD that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Fmr1 cell autonomously promotes maturation of callosal excitatory synapses between somatosensory barrel cortices in mice.
source: Here, we show that Fmr1, whose loss-of-function leads to Fragile X Syndrome (FXS), cell autonomously promotes maturation of callosal excitatory synapses between somatosensory barrel cortices in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including optogenetic stimulation experiments and electrophysiology recordings.

claim: Postnatal, cell-autonomous deletion of Fmr1 in postsynaptic Layer 2/3 or L5 neurons results in a selective weakening of AMPA receptor-mediated callosal synaptic function.
source: Postnatal, cell-autonomous deletion of Fmr1 in postsynaptic Layer (L) 2/3 or L5 neurons results in a selective weakening of AMPA receptor- (R), but not NMDA receptor-, mediated callosal synaptic function, indicative of immature synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiology recordings comparing AMPAR and NMDAR-mediated EPSCs.

claim: Postnatal, cell-autonomous deletion of Fmr1 in postsynaptic Layer 2/3 or L5 neurons does not affect NMDA receptor-mediated callosal synaptic function.
source: Postnatal, cell-autonomous deletion of Fmr1 in postsynaptic Layer (L) 2/3 or L5 neurons results in a selective weakening of AMPA receptor- (R), but not NMDA receptor-, mediated callosal synaptic function, indicative of immature synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiology recordings showing normal NMDAR-mediated EPSCs in Fmr1 KO neurons.

claim: Sensory deprivation by contralateral whisker trimming normalizes callosal input strength in Fmr1 KO L2/3 neurons.
source: Sensory deprivation by contralateral whisker trimming normalizes callosal input strength, suggesting that experience-driven activity of postsynaptic Fmr1 KO L2/3 neurons weakens callosal synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whisker trimming experiments showing normalized callosal synaptic strength.

claim: Experience-driven activity of postsynaptic Fmr1 KO L2/3 neurons weakens callosal synapses.
source: Sensory deprivation by contralateral whisker trimming normalizes callosal input strength, suggesting that experience-driven activity of postsynaptic Fmr1 KO L2/3 neurons weakens callosal synapses.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the whisker trimming experiments showing that preventing sensory-driven activity normalizes callosal inputs.

claim: Synapses originating from local L4 and L2/3 circuits are normal in L2/3 neurons with postsynaptic Fmr1 deletion.
source: In contrast to callosal inputs, synapses originating from local L4 and L2/3 circuits are normal, revealing an input-specific role for postsynaptic Fmr1 in regulation of synaptic connectivity within local and callosal neocortical circuits.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from LSPS experiments showing no difference in local circuit inputs.

claim: Postsynaptic Fmr1 has an input-specific role in regulation of synaptic connectivity within local and callosal neocortical circuits.
source: In contrast to callosal inputs, synapses originating from local L4 and L2/3 circuits are normal, revealing an input-specific role for postsynaptic Fmr1 in regulation of synaptic connectivity within local and callosal neocortical circuits.
evidence: This claim is based on the differential effects observed on callosal versus local inputs in the experimental data.

claim: Reduced corpus callosum integrity and interhemispheric functional connectivity correlates with autistic symptoms in ASD.
source: A common finding in ASD is reduced corpus callosum integrity and interhemispheric functional connectivity, the latter of which correlates with autistic symptoms (Li et al., 2019; O'Reilly et al., 2017; Yao et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The corpus callosum connects bilateral hemispheres and functions to synchronize cortical circuits necessary for sensory-motor processing, attention, perception and higher cognitive functions.
source: The corpus callosum connects bilateral hemispheres and functions to synchronize cortical circuits necessary for sensory-motor processing, attention, perception and higher cognitive functions (Schulte and Müller-Oehring, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research and represents established knowledge.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in FMR1 in humans cause Fragile X Syndrome (FXS), the most common inherited form of intellectual disability and leading monogenic cause of ASD.
source: Loss-of-function mutations in FMR1 in humans cause Fragile X Syndrome (FXS), the most common inherited form of intellectual disability and leading monogenic cause of ASD (Garber et al., 2008; Niu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Children, age 6–24 months, with FXS have reduced structural integrity of white matter tracts, including the corpus callosum.
source: Children, age 6–24 months, with FXS have reduced structural integrity of white matter tracts, including the corpus callosum (Swanson et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Fmr1 knockout (KO) mice have a reduction in white matter tract integrity.
source: Fmr1 knockout (KO) mice, an animal model for FXS, have a similar reduction in white matter tract integrity as well as decreased functional coherence among different cortical regions as measured with functional MRI (Haberl et al., 2015; Zerbi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Fmr1 knockout (KO) mice have decreased functional coherence among different cortical regions as measured with functional MRI.
source: Fmr1 knockout (KO) mice, an animal model for FXS, have a similar reduction in white matter tract integrity as well as decreased functional coherence among different cortical regions as measured with functional MRI (Haberl et al., 2015; Zerbi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neural networks involved in sensory processing show severe functional underconnectivity in Fmr1 KO mice, including both intra- and inter-hemispheric cortical circuits.
source: Specifically, neural networks involved in sensory processing show severe functional underconnectivity, including both intra- and inter-hemispheric cortical circuits (Zerbi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: There are reports of increased connectivity and hyperexcitability of local cortical circuits in humans with ASD and FXS.
source: In addition to reduced long-range connectivity, there are reports of increased connectivity and hyperexcitability of local cortical circuits in humans with ASD and FXS (Ciarrusta et al., 2020; Courchesne and Pierce, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There is strong evidence for hyperexcitable local cortical circuits in the Fmr1 KO mouse, including in visual, auditory, and somatosensory cortices.
source: In the Fmr1 KO mouse, there is strong evidence for hyperexcitable local cortical circuits , including in visual, auditory, and somatosensory cortices (Contractor et al., 2015; Gibson et al., 2008; Gonçalves et al., 2013; Hays et al., 2011; Osterweil et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Hyperactive cortical circuits are observed in humans with FXS and Fmr1 KO mice as an increase in resting state gamma power in the resting state EEG.
source: Hyperactive cortical circuits are also observed in humans with FXS, and Fmr1 KO mice as an increase in resting state gamma power in the resting state EEG (Jonak et al., 2020; Lovelace et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Multiple cellular and synaptic alterations likely contribute to hyperexcitability of local circuits including synaptically hyperconnected pyramidal neurons, reduced inhibitory neuron activity and changes in intrinsic excitability.
source: Multiple cellular and synaptic alterations likely contribute to hyperexcitability of local circuits including synaptically hyperconnected pyramidal neurons, reduced inhibitory neuron activity and changes in intrinsic excitability (Gibson et al., 2008; Goel et al., 2018; He et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and represents a synthesis of multiple findings.

claim: Layer 2/3 and L5 cortical pyramidal neurons receive and integrate excitatory synaptic inputs from homotopic contralateral hemisphere (callosal) as well as other long-range inputs from ipsilateral cortical regions and local cortical circuits.
source: Layer (L) 2/3 and L5 cortical pyramidal neurons receive and integrate excitatory synaptic inputs from homotopic contralateral hemisphere (callosal) as well as other long-range inputs from ipsilateral cortical regions and local cortical circuits.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about cortical circuit organization.

claim: Fmr1 encodes Fragile X Mental Retardation Protein (FMRP), an RNA-binding protein that interacts with many mRNAs including those encoding pre- and post-synaptic proteins.
source: Fmr1 encodes Fragile X Mental Retardation Protein (FMRP), an RNA-binding protein that interacts with many mRNAs including those encoding pre- and post-synaptic proteins (Darnell et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research and represents established knowledge.

claim: FMRP regulates multiple properties of synapses, including maturation, pruning and acute forms of synaptic plasticity.
source: It is perhaps through this diversity of mRNA targets that FMRP regulates multiple properties of synapses, including maturation, pruning and acute forms of synaptic plasticity (Huang et al., 2013; Pfeiffer and Huber, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and involves inference about the mechanism.

claim: Fmr1 regulates maturation of thalamocortical inputs to L4 neurons in somatosensory cortex.
source: Regarding excitatory cortical synapses in somatosensory cortex, Fmr1 regulates maturation of thalamocortical inputs to L4 neurons as well as between local cortical circuits.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research mentioned in the broader context.

claim: A common finding is a delayed maturation of excitatory synapses on Fmr1 KO neurons, as observed by the delayed presence of NMDA receptor-only, or 'silent', synapses and acquisition of AMPAR-mediated synaptic transmission at thalamocortical synapses onto L4 neurons and between locally connected L5 neurons.
source: A common finding is a delayed maturation of excitatory synapses on Fmr1 KO neurons, as observed by the delayed presence of NMDA receptor-only, or 'silent', synapses and acquisition of AMPAR-mediated synaptic transmission at thalamocortical synapses onto L4 neurons and between locally connected L5 neurons (Contractor et al., 2015; Patel et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: L4 to L2/3 synaptic inputs are weak and delayed in their developmental strengthening in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Furthermore, L4 to L2/3 synaptic inputs are weak and delayed in their developmental strengthening, and dendritic spines on cortical pyramidal neurons are thin and filopodial-like, resembling immature spines (Cruz-Martín et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2013; Nimchinsky et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Dendritic spines on cortical pyramidal neurons in Fmr1 KO mice are thin and filopodial-like, resembling immature spines.
source: Furthermore, L4 to L2/3 synaptic inputs are weak and delayed in their developmental strengthening, and dendritic spines on cortical pyramidal neurons are thin and filopodial-like, resembling immature spines (Cruz-Martín et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2013; Nimchinsky et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: L5 local synaptic connections ultimately mature and appear normal during the 4th postnatal week but then fail to prune, which results in hyperconnectivity of L5 neurons at 4–5 weeks of age in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: L5 local synaptic connections ultimately mature and appear normal during the 4th postnatal week but then fail to prune, which results in hyperconnectivity of L5 neurons at 4–5 weeks of age as compared to wild-type cortex (Patel et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The delayed development and hyperconnectivity of L5 circuits are due to a cell autonomous, postsynaptic role for FMRP in L5 neurons.
source: Importantly, the delayed development and hyperconnectivity of L5 circuits are due to a cell autonomous, postsynaptic role for FMRP in L5 neurons, suggesting a direct role of FMRP in coordinating multiple synapse development processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research and involves inference about the mechanism.

claim: The amplitude of LED-evoked EPSCs in Fmr1 KO neurons was reduced by ~40% compared to WT.
source: The amplitude of LED-evoked EPSCs in Fmr1 KO neurons was reduced by ~40 % compared to WT.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Callosal synaptic inputs onto WT L2/3 neurons are strongest at the proximal apical dendrites.
source: Results reveal that callosal synaptic inputs onto WT L2/3 neurons are strongest at the proximal apical dendrites (Figure 1H), consistent with previous reports (Petreanu et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and is consistent with previous research.

claim: There is an interaction of Fmr1 and vertical position in the distribution of callosal synaptic inputs.
source: Results reveal that callosal synaptic inputs onto WT L2/3 neurons are strongest at the proximal apical dendrites (Figure 1H), consistent with previous reports (Petreanu et al., 2009) and there is an interaction of Fmr1 and vertical position (*p < 0.05, F(15, 849) = 1.723; mixed-effects ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Comparison of mean EPSC amplitudes from proximal apical dendrites reveals a 50% reduction in callosal synaptic input strength in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Comparison of mean EPSC amplitudes from proximal apical dendrites reveals a 50 % reduction in callosal synaptic input strength in Fmr1 KO mice (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: At P18-20, overall callosal synaptic input strengths were not different between WT and postsynaptic Fmr1 KO neurons.
source: Interestingly, at the earliest age for recording (P18-20), overall callosal synaptic input strengths were not different between WT and postsynaptic Fmr1 KO neurons (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: At P23-30, postsynaptic Fmr1 KO neurons had a 40% reduction in callosal synaptic input strength compared to neighboring WT neurons.
source: However, at P23-30, postsynaptic Fmr1 KO neurons had a 40 % reduction in callosal synaptic input strength compared to neighboring WT neurons (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A two-way ANOVA indicates a significant interaction between genotype and age for callosal synaptic input strength.
source: A two-way ANOVA indicates a significant interaction between genotype and age (Fmr1 x Age ***p < 0.001, F(1, 32) = 13.87)(Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There is a strong trend of callosal input strength to increase with developmental age in WT, but not Fmr1 KO, neurons.
source: In addition, we observed a strong trend of callosal input strength to increase with developmental age in WT, but not Fmr1 KO, neurons (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Fmr1 in postsynaptic L2/3 neurons cell-autonomously promotes the development and/or strengthening of callosal synaptic inputs.
source: These data demonstrate that Fmr1 in postsynaptic L2/3 neurons cell-autonomously promotes the development and/or strengthening of callosal synaptic inputs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing differential effects in WT versus Fmr1 KO neurons.

claim: In adult mice (P57-65), callosal mediated EPSCs were weak in Fmr1 KO neurons; reduced by 25%, in comparison to WT neurons.
source: Similar to young mice, callosal mediated EPSCs were weak in Fmr1 KO neurons; reduced by 25%, in comparison to WT neurons (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: Weak callosal synaptic transmission persists into adulthood with postsynaptic Fmr1 deletion.
source: These results indicate that weak callosal synaptic transmission persists into adulthood with postsynaptic Fmr1 deletion.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing persistent deficits in adult mice.

claim: Postsynaptic Fmr1 KO neurons received >20% fewer evoked events in Sr2+ in comparison to neighboring WT neurons with no change in event amplitude.
source: Postsynaptic Fmr1 KO neurons received >20% fewer evoked events in Sr2+ in comparison to neighboring WT neurons with no change in event amplitude (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: The baseline frequency and amplitude of spontaneous EPSCs, prior to LED stimulation, were not different between genotypes.
source: The baseline frequency and amplitude of spontaneous EPSCs, prior to LED stimulation, were not different between genotypes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The reduced EPSCs onto postsynaptic Fmr1 KO neurons are a consequence of reduced presynaptic release probability, functional synapse number or both.
source: These results suggest the reduced EPSCs onto postsynaptic Fmr1 KO neurons are a consequence of reduced presynaptic release probability, functional synapse number or both.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the Sr2+ experiment results.

claim: C.V. is inversely proportional to release probability and synapse number.
source: C.V. is inversely proportional to release probability and synapse number (Manabe et al., 1993)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research and represents established knowledge.

claim: C.V. was increased by 18% in Fmr1 KO neurons.
source: C.V. is inversely proportional to release probability and synapse number (Manabe et al., 1993) and was increased by 18 % in Fmr1 KO neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The weakening of callosal-mediated EPSCs in Fmr1 KO is due in part to decreased synapse number and/or presynaptic release probability.
source: This result together with reduced frequency of events evoked in Sr2+ indicate that the weakening of callosal-mediated EPSCs in Fmr1 KO is due in part to decreased synapse number and/or presynaptic release probability.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results including Sr2+ experiments and C.V. measurements.

claim: Amplitudes of NMDAR EPSCs evoked from callosal axons were not different between WT and neighboring postsynaptic Fmr1 KO neurons.
source: In contrast to AMPAR-mediated EPSCs, amplitudes of NMDAR EPSCs evoked from callosal axons were not different between WT and neighboring postsynaptic Fmr1 KO neurons (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The NMDAR content within callosal synapses are similar for WT and KO neurons.
source: This observation suggests that the NMDAR content within callosal synapses are similar for WT and KO neurons and that there is no change in presynaptic release probability or synapse number for the callosal axons.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the NMDAR EPSC data.

claim: There is no change in presynaptic release probability or synapse number for the callosal axons onto Fmr1 KO neurons.
source: This observation suggests that the NMDAR content within callosal synapses are similar for WT and KO neurons and that there is no change in presynaptic release probability or synapse number for the callosal axons.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the NMDAR EPSC data combined with AMPAR EPSC data.

claim: L2/3 Fmr1 KO neurons have an increased proportion of synapses with NMDARs, but not functional AMPARs, indicative of immature synapses.
source: Taken together with the reduced frequency of AMPAR quantal events and increased C.V. (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), our results suggest that L2/3 Fmr1 KO neurons have an increased proportion of synapses with NMDARs, but not functional AMPARs, indicative of immature synapses.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results including AMPAR and NMDAR measurements.

claim: L2/3 pyramidal neurons with postsynaptic Fmr1 deletion have a 45% reduction in callosal synaptic input strength as compared to neighboring WT neurons with action potential-evoked synaptic transmission.
source: Quantification of mean EPSC amplitude within the region covering the soma and major dendrites shows that L2/3 pyramidal neurons with postsynaptic Fmr1 deletion have a 45 % reduction in callosal synaptic input strength as compared to neighboring WT neurons (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: L5 pyramidal neurons with postsynaptic Fmr1 deletion have a 40% reduction in the strength of callosal inputs stimulated around the soma and apical dendrites.
source: Similar to L2/3, L5 pyramidal neurons with postsynaptic Fmr1 deletion have a 40 % reduction in the strength of callosal inputs stimulated around the soma and apical dendrites (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Postsynaptic deletion of Fmr1 in pyramidal cortical neurons generally weakens callosal synaptic inputs and this is observed with action potential driven synaptic transmission and across different layers.
source: Together, these results show that postsynaptic deletion of Fmr1 in pyramidal cortical neurons generally weakens callosal synaptic inputs and this is observed with action potential driven synaptic transmission and across different layers.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data across L2/3 and L5 neurons.

claim: Targeting, branching and elaboration of callosal axons into the contralateral neocortex occurs postnatally (~P5-15) and depends on activity of presynaptic and postsynaptic cortical neurons as well as whisker sensory experience.
source: Targeting, branching and elaboration of callosal axons into the contralateral neocortex occurs postnatally (~P5-15) and depends on activity of presynaptic and postsynaptic cortical neurons as well as whisker sensory experience (Huang et al., 2013; Mizuno et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In the 'presynaptic deprivation' condition, callosal synaptic input strength was weak (27% reduction) onto postsynaptic Fmr1 KO L2/3 neurons as compared to WT.
source: In the 'presynaptic deprivation' condition, callosal synaptic input strength was weak (27 % reduction) onto postsynaptic Fmr1 KO L2/3 neurons as compared to WT, similar to that observed in whisker intact mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whisker trimming experiments.

claim: In the 'postsynaptic deprivation' condition, callosal synaptic inputs strengths were similar between WT and Fmr1 KO neurons.
source: In contrast, in the 'postsynaptic deprivation' condition, callosal synaptic inputs strengths were similar between WT and Fmr1 KO neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whisker trimming experiments.

claim: A two-way ANOVA revealed an interaction of deprivation condition and Fmr1 for callosal synaptic input strength.
source: A two-way ANOVA revealed an interaction of deprivation condition and Fmr1 (*p < 0.05, F(1, 31) = 4.977, ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Callosal synaptic input strengths in WT neurons were not different between deprivation conditions.
source: Surprisingly, callosal synaptic input strengths in WT neurons were not different between deprivation conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whisker trimming experiments.

claim: In Fmr1 KO neurons callosal input strengths were weaker, decreased by ~45%, in the presynaptic deprivation condition, as compared to postsynaptic deprivation.
source: In contrast, in Fmr1 KO neurons callosal input strengths were weaker, decreased by ~45%, in the presynaptic deprivation condition, as compared to postsynaptic deprivation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whisker trimming experiments.

claim: Whisker experience-driven activity of postsynaptic Fmr1 KO L2/3 neurons weakens callosal synaptic inputs.
source: These data suggest that whisker experience-driven activity of postsynaptic Fmr1 KO L2/3 neurons weakens callosal synaptic inputs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the whisker trimming experimental results.

claim: A previous study reported weak L4 to L2/3 synaptic inputs in the barrel cortex of global Fmr1 KO mice.
source: A previous study reported weak L4 to L2/3 synaptic inputs in the barrel cortex of global Fmr1 KO mice (Bureau et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: EPSCs evoked from L4 home or adjacent barrels, L5A or L2/3 were unaffected on Fmr1 KO L2/3 neurons.
source: EPSCs evoked from L4 home or adjacent barrels, L5A or L2/3 were unaffected on Fmr1 KO L2/3 neurons (Figure 6E), in contrast to the weak EPSCs from callosal inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Local synaptic input strength from L4 home barrel measured at P14-17 is not affected by sparse deletion of Fmr1 in L2/3 neurons using AAV.GFP-Cre injection at P1.
source: To test if loss of postsynaptic Fmr1 weakens local L4 to L2/3 synaptic inputs at early developmental stages, we performed LSPS on pairs of WT and postsynaptic Fmr1 KO L2/3 pyramidal neurons at P14-17. Similar to results obtained at P23-30, we observed normal L4 and adjacent L2/3 synaptic input strengths onto postsynaptic Fmr1 L2/3 neurons recorded at P14-17 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Embryonic deletion of postsynaptic Fmr1 using mosaic Fmr1 females does not affect L4 input strengths onto L2/3 neurons at P14-17.
source: We also tested if embryonic deletion of postsynaptic Fmr1 was necessary to affect L4 to L2/3 synapse development, using slices from females with heterozygous (het) and mosaic expression of Fmr1, as we have described (Patel et al., 2013; Patel et al., 2014). Briefly, X-linked GFP mice were bred with Fmr1 KO males. Due to random X-chromosome inactivation in the embryo, female Fmr1 het mice offspring have a mosaic expression of GFP(+) WT and GFP(-) Fmr1 KO neurons. LSPS maps were performed on pairs of WT and Fmr1 KO neurons at P14-17 where we observed normal L4 input strengths onto L2/3 Fmr1 KO neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Weak L4 to L2/3 synaptic inputs in the global Fmr1 KO is not a postsynaptic, cell autonomous function of FMRP, but instead is either a non-cell autonomous function of FMRP or a role in presynaptic L4 neurons.
source: Although synaptic inputs from L4 to L2/3 are weak in the global Fmr1 KO, this is not a postsynaptic, cell autonomous function of FMRP, but instead is either a non-cell autonomous function of FMRP or a role in presynaptic L4 neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from comparing results of postsynaptic deletion versus global KO.

claim: Reduced interhemispheric connectivity, observed both structurally and functionally, is a hallmark of ASD in humans and correlated with symptoms.
source: Reduced interhemispheric connectivity, observed both structurally and functionally, is a hallmark of ASD in humans and correlated with symptoms (Dimond et al., 2019; Holiga et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019; O'Reilly et al., 2017; Rane et al., 2015; Yao et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Fmr1 KO mice have reduced corticocortical long-range connectivity, especially among the sensory and motor cortices.
source: Functional MRI studies show that Fmr1 KO mice have reduced corticocortical long-range connectivity, especially among the sensory and motor cortices (Haberl et al., 2015; Zerbi et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Fmr1 KO mice have reduced corpus callosum structural integrity.
source: Functional MRI studies show that Fmr1 KO mice have reduced corticocortical long-range connectivity, especially among the sensory and motor cortices (Haberl et al., 2015; Zerbi et al., 2018) as well as reduced corpus callosum structural integrity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Reduced functional coherence between bilateral barrel cortices in Fmr1 KO mice could be due to a disrupted communication between the cortices through the weakened monosynaptic transmission.
source: This result suggests that reduced functional coherence between bilateral barrel cortices in Fmr1 KO mice could be due to a disrupted communication between the cortices through the weakened monosynaptic transmission.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing weak callosal synapses.

claim: Interhemispheric functional connectivity is thought to shape perceptual integration including those involved in speech comprehension and global form processing, domains that are impaired in ASD.
source: Interhemispheric functional connectivity is thought to shape perceptual integration including those involved in speech comprehension and global form processing, domains that are impaired in ASD (Booth and Happé, 2018; Friederici et al., 2007; Happé and Frith, 2006; Peiker et al., 2015; Preisig et al., 2021; Simon and Wallace, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It is likely that FMRP promotes other 'long-range' synaptic connections between cortical areas, such as ipsilateral connectivity between S1 and M1/M2, as well as cortical-subcortical structures.
source: Based on fMRI results in the Fmr1 KO (Haberl et al., 2015; Zerbi et al., 2018), it is likely that FMRP promotes other 'long-range' synaptic connections between cortical areas, such as ipsilateral connectivity between S1 and M1/M2, as well as cortical-subcortical structures.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation and inference from fMRI results cited.

claim: Callosal synaptic strength tends to increase from P18-20 to P23-30 in WT neurons but not in postsynaptic Fmr1 KO neurons.
source: In support of a role in maturation, callosal synaptic strength tends to increase from P18-20 to P23-30 in WT neurons but not in postsynaptic Fmr1 KO neurons (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Thalamocortical inputs to L4 are delayed in their development in the Fmr1 KO, as measured by acquisition of AMPARs.
source: Although we did not measure 'silent' callosal synapses here, our findings would predict more 'silent' and immature callosal synapses in Fmr1 KO L2/3 neurons. In support of this idea, thalamocortical inputs to L4, another 'long-range' synaptic pathway, are delayed in their development in the Fmr1 KO, as measured by acquisition of AMPARs (Harlow et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The optogenetic stimulation paradigm used to evoke glutamate release from callosal axons may saturate synaptic NMDARs, but not AMPARs, due to the higher affinity of glutamate for NMDARs.
source: Another possible explanation for our results is the optogenetic stimulation paradigm we used to evoke glutamate release from callosal axons saturates synaptic NMDARs, but not AMPARs, due to the higher affinity of glutamate for NMDARs (Patneau and Mayer, 1990).
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about a possible alternative explanation, supported by a citation about glutamate affinity.

claim: Reduced corpus callosum structural integrity and interhemispheric coherence with fMRI are observed in adult Fmr1 KO.
source: The observations of reduced corpus callosum structural integrity and interhemispheric coherence with fMRI in adult Fmr1 KO suggest weak callosal connectivity in adults (Haberl et al., 2015; Zerbi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Reduced callosal axon diameter is observed in adult Fmr1 KO which may be a consequence of weak or immature callosal synapses and contribute to reduced interhemispheric coherence in FXS.
source: Reduced callosal axon diameter is observed in adult Fmr1 KO which may be a consequence of weak or immature callosal synapses and contribute to reduced interhemispheric coherence in FXS (Haberl et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on inference and speculation about the relationship between synaptic weakness and axon diameter, supported by a citation.

claim: An imbalance in local and long-range connectivity has been hypothesized to contribute to ASD in humans; specifically, hyperconnectivity of local circuits and underconnectivity of long-range circuits or between brain regions.
source: In addition to reduced long-range connectivity, there are reports of increased connectivity and hyperexcitability of local cortical circuits in humans with ASD and FXS (Ciarrusta et al., 2020; Courchesne and Pierce, 2005). In the Fmr1 KO mouse, there is strong evidence for hyperexcitable local cortical circuits , including in visual, auditory, and somatosensory cortices (Contractor et al., 2015; Gibson et al., 2008; Gonçalves et al., 2013; Hays et al., 2011; Osterweil et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and represents a hypothesis in the field.

claim: Postsynaptic FMRP differentially regulates development and/or maintenance of synaptic inputs from local and long-range cortical sources.
source: Here we demonstrate that postsynaptic FMRP differentially regulates development and/or maintenance of synaptic inputs from local and long-range cortical sources.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing differential effects on callosal versus local inputs.

claim: L2/3 neurons with postsynaptic deletion of Fmr1 have weak and immature callosal synaptic inputs but normal synaptic inputs from L4, adjacent L2/3 and L5.
source: L2/3 neurons with postsynaptic deletion of Fmr1 have weak and immature callosal synaptic inputs but normal synaptic inputs from L4, adjacent L2/3 and L5 (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Weak L4 to L2/3 synapses in the global Fmr1 KO suggest a role for FMRP in presynaptic L4 neurons in synapse development onto L2/3 neurons.
source: Bureau et al. (Bureau et al., 2008) and we (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) find that L4 to L2/3 synapses are weak in the global Fmr1 KO, but we do not observe this with embryonic or postnatal cell autonomous deletion of Fmr1 in L2/3 neurons. Together these results suggest a role for FMRP in presynaptic L4 neurons in synapse development onto L2/3 neurons, which is consistent with the reported deficits in L4 axon morphology in the global Fmr1 KO (Bureau et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from comparing results across different experimental conditions and is supported by citations.

claim: Hyperconnectivity of L5 local subnetworks in Fmr1 KO resulted from deficient developmental pruning between Fmr1 KO L5 neurons and was observed in both the global Fmr1 KO and with postsynaptic Fmr1 deletion.
source: Our previous work using multiple simultaneous recordings of locally connected L5A neurons, revealed hyperconnectivity of Fmr1 KO L5 neurons with their immediate neighbors ( < 40 µm apart) in S1 at 4 weeks of age (Patel et al., 2014). Hyperconnectivity of L5 local subnetworks resulted from deficient developmental pruning between Fmr1 KO L5 neurons and was observed in both the global Fmr1 KO and with postsynaptic Fmr1 deletion.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Prefrontal L5 cortical neurons in Fmr1 KO mice are hyperconnected.
source: Prefrontal L5 cortical neurons in Fmr1 KO mice are similarly hyperconnected (Testa-Silva et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Postsynaptic deletion of Fmr1 in L5 neurons results in weak callosal synaptic inputs.
source: In contrast to local hyperconnectivity, here we find that postsynaptic deletion of Fmr1 in L5 neurons results in weak callosal synaptic inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Fmr1 KO L5 pyramidal neurons are hyperconnected locally and under-connected to contralateral cortex; an effect that is mediated by cell-autonomous and postsynaptic deletion of FMRP.
source: Thus, Fmr1 KO L5 pyramidal neurons are hyperconnected locally and under-connected to contralateral cortex; an effect that is mediated by cell-autonomous and postsynaptic deletion of FMRP.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing differential effects on local versus callosal connectivity.

claim: The imbalance in local and long-range functional connectivity in L5 neurons may promote the reported imbalances in local and long-range functional connectivity observed in ASD individuals.
source: Such an effect may promote the reported imbalances in local and long-range functional connectivity observed in ASD individuals.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: Postsynaptic deletion of FMRP in L2/3 neurons did not affect synaptic inputs from other layers or between columns within L2/3.
source: Postsynaptic deletion of FMRP in L2/3 neurons did not affect synaptic inputs from other layers or between columns within L2/3 (Figure 6)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: FMRP may selectively promote pruning of local connections in L5 neurons.
source: Postsynaptic deletion of FMRP in L2/3 neurons did not affect synaptic inputs from other layers or between columns within L2/3 (Figure 6) suggesting that FMRP may selectively promote pruning of local connections in L5 neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation and inference from the differential effects observed.

claim: FMRP may prune synaptic connections within very local cortical subnetworks (within 40 µm) in both L2/3 and L5, but not connections between layers and columns.
source: Alternatively, FMRP may prune synaptic connections within very local cortical subnetworks (within 40 µm) in both L2/3 and L5, but not connections between layers and columns.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about an alternative explanation for the observed results.

claim: L4 neurons synapse primarily on basal dendrites of L2/3 neurons, whereas callosal inputs are primarily on apical dendrites.
source: L4 neurons synapse primarily on basal dendrites of L2/3 neurons, whereas callosal inputs are primarily on apical dendrites (Bosman et al., 2011; Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research and experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Localized expression and translational regulation of specific dendritic mRNAs by FMRP at either basal or apical dendritic compartments could differentially affect L4 and callosal inputs.
source: Therefore, localized expression and translational regulation of specific dendritic mRNAs by FMRP at either basal or apical dendritic compartments could differentially affect L4 and callosal inputs.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about a possible molecular mechanism.

claim: FMRP translational regulation of postsynaptic cell adhesion molecules, such as neuroligins, could differentially impact specific presynaptic inputs based on their expression of binding partners such as neurexin splice variants.
source: Alternatively, FMRP translational regulation of postsynaptic cell adhesion molecules, such as neuroligins, could differentially impact specific presynaptic inputs based on their expression of binding partners such as neurexin splice variants (Südhof, 2017).
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about a possible molecular mechanism, supported by a citation.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in MEF2C are implicated in intellectual disability, ASD and schizophrenia.
source: Loss-of-function mutations in MEF2C, which encodes an activity-dependent transcription factor, are implicated in intellectual disability, ASD and schizophrenia (Assali et al., 2019; Mitchell et al., 2018; Rocha et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Postsynaptic deletion of Mef2c in L2/3 neurons results in fewer and weak inputs from local circuits (L4, L2/3, and L5), but strengthened callosal inputs.
source: In contrast to FMRP, postsynaptic deletion of Mef2c in L2/3 neurons results in fewer and weak inputs from local circuits (L4, L2/3, and L5), but strengthened callosal inputs (Rajkovich et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The differential regulation of local and callosal synaptic connections by postsynaptic MEF2C and FMRP suggest that imbalances in local and long-range synaptic connectivity may contribute to different genetic causes of neurodevelopmental disorders.
source: The differential regulation of local and callosal synaptic connections by postsynaptic MEF2C and FMRP, albeit in different directions, suggest that imbalances in local and long-range synaptic connectivity may contribute to different genetic causes of neurodevelopmental disorders.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from comparing the effects of different genes.

claim: Bidirectional regulation of local and long-range connectivity by Mef2c in L2/3 or by Fmr1 in L5 could be an effect of homeostasis or competition between local and long-range synaptic connections to maintain optimal cortical circuit function.
source: Bidirectional regulation of local and long-range connectivity by Mef2c in L2/3 or by Fmr1 in L5 could be an effect of homeostasis or competition between local and long-range synaptic connections to maintain optimal cortical circuit function.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about a possible mechanism.

claim: Weakening of callosal synaptic input in Fmr1 KO neurons may be compensatory and an attempt to normalize hyperconnected or hyperexcitable local circuits.
source: For example, weakening of callosal synaptic input in Fmr1 KO neurons may be compensatory and an attempt to normalize hyperconnected or hyperexcitable local circuits.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about a possible compensatory mechanism.

claim: The regulation of local or callosal connectivity by FMRP and MEF2C requires normal sensory experience.
source: The regulation of local or callosal connectivity by FMRP and MEF2C requires normal sensory experience suggesting that both of these genes function in experience and activity-regulated pathways necessary for cortical circuit development.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental results showing effects of sensory deprivation.

claim: Both FMRP and MEF2C function in experience and activity-regulated pathways necessary for cortical circuit development.
source: The regulation of local or callosal connectivity by FMRP and MEF2C requires normal sensory experience suggesting that both of these genes function in experience and activity-regulated pathways necessary for cortical circuit development.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental results.

claim: Sensory deprivation by whisker trimming normalizes callosal synaptic inputs in L2/3 neurons with postsynaptic deletion of Fmr1 or Mef2c.
source: Sensory deprivation by whisker trimming normalizes callosal synaptic inputs in L2/3 neurons with postsynaptic deletion of Fmr1 (Figure 4) or Mef2c (Rajkovich et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and a citation to previous research.

claim: Trimming whiskers contralateral to L2/3 neurons with postsynaptic Fmr1 deletion (postsynaptic deprivation) prevented callosal synaptic weakening.
source: Specifically, trimming whiskers contralateral to L2/3 neurons with postsynaptic Fmr1 deletion (postsynaptic deprivation) prevented callosal synaptic weakening.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whisker trimming experiments.

claim: 'Presynaptic deprivation' or trimming whiskers contralateral to ChR2-expressing, callosal projecting neurons, had no effect on callosal synaptic strength.
source: In contrast, 'presynaptic deprivation' or trimming whiskers contralateral to ChR2-expressing, callosal projecting neurons, had no effect (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Sensory-driven patterned activity of postsynaptic Fmr1 KO L2/3 neurons weakens callosal synapses.
source: This result suggests that sensory-driven patterned activity of postsynaptic Fmr1 KO L2/3 neurons weakens callosal synapses.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the whisker trimming experimental results.

claim: An activity-dependent long-term synaptic depression (LTD) process may be enhanced at Fmr1 KO L2/3 neurons as observed in hippocampal CA1.
source: An intriguing possibility is that an activity-dependent long-term synaptic depression (LTD) process is enhanced at Fmr1 KO L2/3 neurons as observed in hippocampal CA1 (Huber et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about a possible mechanism, supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Sensory deprivation induces homeostatic synaptic scaling in primary sensory cortices, as measured with spontaneous or miniature (m) EPSCs.
source: Sensory deprivation also induces homeostatic synaptic scaling in primary sensory cortices, as measured with spontaneous or miniature (m) EPSCs (Feldman, 2009; Hooks and Chen, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and represents established knowledge.

claim: Neither the frequency nor amplitude of mEPSCs was different between neighboring WT and Fmr1 KO L2/3 neurons in mice with normal sensory experience or 'presynaptic deprivation'.
source: Neither the frequency nor amplitude of mEPSCs was different between neighboring WT and Fmr1 KO L2/3 neurons in mice with normal sensory experience or 'presynaptic deprivation'.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: With 'postsynaptic deprivation', mEPSC amplitude and frequency was increased in Fmr1 KO neurons relative to WT.
source: However, with 'postsynaptic deprivation', mEPSC amplitude and frequency was increased in Fmr1 KO neurons relative to WT (Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Homeostatic up scaling in Fmr1 KO neurons with postsynaptic deprivation may contribute to callosal input strengthening in this condition.
source: However, with 'postsynaptic deprivation', mEPSC amplitude and frequency was increased in Fmr1 KO neurons relative to WT (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) suggestive of homeostatic up scaling in Fmr1 KO neurons that may contribute to callosal input strengthening in this condition.
evidence: This claim is based on inference and speculation from the mEPSC data.

claim: Bilateral underconnectivity is common in ASD as well as disconnection of other long-range cortical connections with other brain regions such as hippocampus and cerebellum.
source: Bilateral underconnectivity is common in ASD as well as disconnection of other long-range cortical connections with other brain regions such as hippocampus and cerebellum.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in the field of ASD research.

claim: Bilateral connectivity and synchrony between cortical regions are necessary for speech comprehension, sensory processing, and cognition, domains impaired in FXS and ASD.
source: Bilateral connectivity and synchrony between cortical regions are necessary for speech comprehension, sensory processing, and cognition (Bland et al., 2020; Castro et al., 2014; Friederici et al., 2007; Fries, 2009; Fries, 2015; Panzica et al., 2019), domains impaired in FXS and ASD.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.
